central_question: By 31 Dec 2027, will NVIDIA retain >= 75% revenue share of the data-center AI accelerator (training+inference silicon) market, or will hyperscaler custom ASICs (Google TPU, AWS Trainium, Microsoft Maia, Meta MTIA) plus AMD Instinct erode NVIDIA below 75%?

situation_brief.current_situation: As of mid-2026 NVIDIA still commands an estimated 80-90% of merchant data-center AI accelerator revenue, anchored by the Blackwell (GB200/GB300) ramp and the CUDA software moat, but the question is whether custom ASIC volumes and AMD Instinct (MI300/MI350/MI400) can pull NVIDIA below 75% by end-2027. Hyperscaler in-house silicon (Google TPU v6/v7, AWS Trainium2/3, Microsoft Maia, Meta MTIA) is scaling fast for internal inference and increasingly training, while HBM and CoWoS-class advanced packaging remain the binding supply constraints.
situation_brief.context: Demand is driven by frontier-model training (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, xAI) and a rapidly growing inference base. The entire stack depends on TSMC leading-edge nodes (N4/N3/N2), CoWoS advanced packaging, and HBM3E/HBM4 from SK Hynix, Samsung, and Micron. US export controls (BIS/Commerce) cap China access to leading-edge AI chips and ASML EUV tools, reshaping demand geography and pushing China toward Huawei Ascend and SMIC domestic capacity.
situation_brief.dynamics: Two opposing forces define the trajectory: (1) NVIDIA's full-stack lock-in (CUDA, NVLink/NVSwitch, networking via Mellanox/Spectrum-X, annual cadence) plus first call on scarce CoWoS and HBM; versus (2) hyperscalers' structural incentive to cut cost-per-token and supply risk by shifting inference (and some training) to internal ASICs co-designed with Broadcom and Marvell. Definitional sensitivity is decisive: if captive ASIC TPU/Trainium/Maia/MTIA volumes count in the denominator at internal transfer value, NVIDIA share compresses faster than in a merchant-only view, so the share math hinges on whether 'merchant silicon' or 'all accelerators including captive ASICs' is the denominator.
fault_lines: Denominator definition: merchant silicon only vs. all accelerators including captive hyperscaler ASICs at internal cost/transfer value
Training (NVIDIA/AMD-dominated, NVLink-scale) vs. inference (where custom ASICs and cheaper parts erode share fastest)
CUDA software lock-in vs. open stacks (ROCm, Triton, JAX/XLA, PyTorch backends, MLIR)
Supply allocation: who gets scarce CoWoS-L/CoWoS-S and HBM4 capacity first
US-China decoupling: export-controlled Western demand vs. Huawei/SMIC domestic substitution
Hyperscaler vertical integration vs. dependence on NVIDIA for frontier-scale training clusters
HBM oligopoly pricing power (SK Hynix/Samsung/Micron) vs. accelerator vendor margins
catalysts: NVIDIA Rubin (R100) launch and 2027 ramp cadence vs. Blackwell Ultra
Google TPU v7 (Ironwood-class) external availability and Anthropic/third-party TPU adoption
AWS Trainium3 ramp and Project Rainier-scale Anthropic clusters
AMD MI400 / Helios rack-scale launch (2026-2027) and ROCm maturity
HBM4 qualification and CoWoS capacity expansions at TSMC through 2027
BIS export-control revisions affecting H20-class/B-series China SKUs
OpenAI custom-silicon program (Broadcom co-design) reaching volume
Microsoft Maia next-gen and Meta MTIA v3 internal deployment milestones

relationships.basis: All NVIDIA leading-edge AI GPUs are fabricated on TSMC nodes with TSMC CoWoS packaging, making capacity allocation a hard ceiling.

Micron is a qualified HBM3E second/third source for NVIDIA platforms, diversifying memory supply.
NVIDIA evaluates Samsung HBM and packaging as secondary supply, contingent on qualification progress.
TSMC's leading-edge nodes require ASML EUV and High-NA lithography, of which ASML is the sole supplier.
Samsung's GAA leading-edge processes depend on ASML EUV systems.
Intel Foundry's 18A/14A roadmap relies on ASML EUV and is an early High-NA EUV customer.

Oracle is a core Stargate partner providing large OCI GPU capacity to OpenAI.
Anthropic depends on Google TPU capacity (reportedly up to ~1M TPUs) for Claude compute.
Anthropic depends on AWS Trainium capacity and AWS funding as primary backer.
Microsoft Azure is among the largest NVIDIA GPU buyers despite developing Maia.
Meta runs one of the largest NVIDIA GPU fleets for Llama training despite deploying MTIA.
BIS export controls restrict which NVIDIA AI GPUs (e.g., H20-class) can ship to China, repeatedly revised.
US-coordinated controls (with the Dutch government) restrict ASML EUV/DUV exports to China.
BIS export thresholds also gate AMD Instinct sales to China.
BIS placed Huawei on the Entity List and targets its access to advanced chips and tools.
BIS restricts SMIC via the Entity List and tool controls to curb advanced-node progress.
BIS export controls restrict EDA sales (Cadence) for advanced-node design to China.
BIS export controls restrict Synopsys EDA/IP for advanced China designs.
MIIT industrial policy and procurement steer Chinese AI demand toward Huawei Ascend.
MIIT and the Big Fund back SMIC's domestic advanced-node capacity expansion.
MIIT reportedly discouraged Chinese firms from buying certain NVIDIA China SKUs to favor domestic chips.
Huawei Ascend accelerators are fabricated on SMIC's DUV-based 7nm-class processes.
Google's TPU program depends on Broadcom co-design and SerDes/packaging IP.
Meta's MTIA accelerators depend on Broadcom co-design.
AWS custom AI silicon depends in part on Marvell co-design and interconnect IP.
Google TPUs are fabricated at TSMC, competing for the same CoWoS/HBM allocation.
AWS Trainium/Inferentia are fabricated at TSMC.
Broadcom's custom XPUs and networking silicon are fabricated and packaged at TSMC.

NVIDIA relies on Cadence EDA tooling for advanced AI chip design.
SK Hynix partners with TSMC on HBM4 base-die logic for tighter accelerator integration.
NVIDIA aligns with and reportedly invests in OpenAI-related compute buildouts to anchor demand.

key_events.event: BIS imposes first sweeping export controls restricting advanced AI GPUs and chipmaking tools to China, forcing NVIDIA to create cut-down China SKUs.
NVIDIA reports a data-center revenue surge as Hopper (H100) demand explodes, kicking off the AI accelerator boom.
BIS tightens controls again, capturing NVIDIA's A800/H800 China parts and prompting the H20 redesign.
Microsoft unveils its Maia 100 AI accelerator and Cobalt Arm CPU, signaling hyperscaler in-housing.
AMD launches Instinct MI300X, establishing the first credible merchant alternative to NVIDIA's data-center GPUs.
NVIDIA announces the Blackwell (GB200 NVL72) platform at GTC, extending its rack-scale and cadence lead.
AWS and Anthropic deepen ties as Amazon commits additional billions and builds Trainium 'Project Rainier' training clusters.
Reports surface that OpenAI is co-designing a custom inference chip with Broadcom on TSMC, signaling lab-level vertical integration.
BIS issues further controls on HBM and advanced tools to China, broadening the chokepoint campaign.
OpenAI, Oracle, and partners announce the Stargate AI-infrastructure initiative, escalating compute-buildout scale.
NVIDIA details Blackwell Ultra (GB300) and teases Rubin (R100) on an annual cadence at GTC 2025.
CoreWeave completes its IPO, crystallizing the leveraged neocloud model built on NVIDIA allocation.
BIS effectively requires licenses for NVIDIA H20 and AMD MI308 China sales, materially curbing China accelerator revenue.
AMD unveils the MI350 series and the MI400/Helios rack-scale roadmap targeting NVIDIA at the system level.
Broadcom guidance and reports point to a fourth major custom-XPU customer (read as OpenAI), reinforcing the ASIC-shift thesis.
At GTC 2026 NVIDIA reaffirms Rubin ramp timing and AI-factory demand, framing the market as still expanding faster than ASIC erosion.
